key_insight: A unified Hamilton-principle-based thermo-mechanical model captures first-order melting and second-order glass transition effects in glass additive manufacturing under extreme thermal histories.
engineering_relevance: The framework helps predict residual stress, warpage, and microstructural freezing during laser-based glass printing, supporting more reliable process and material design.
method: Extended variational formulation coupling heat, mechanics, and phase transformation at finite strains
Kinematic split including thermal expansion, density changes, and viscoelastic deformation
Temperature-dependent viscosity with monolithic NEM heat solution and 3D ANSYS process simulation
evidence_signal: The model was validated at the material-point level against Time-Temperature-Transformation behavior and then demonstrated in 3D deposition simulations showing residual stress buildup and warpage.
watch_item: Accurate deployment depends on reliable phase-kinetics and viscosity calibration, especially under very rapid cooling where small parameter errors can strongly affect predicted vitrification and stress evolution.
paper_title: First- and Second-Order Phase Transformation Modeling Based on the Hamilton Principle: A Coupled Thermo-Mechanical Approach for Glass Additive Manufacturing
